templates.pattern: A habitat patch shrinks from [INIT] km² to [FINAL] km² over [YRS] years due to human activity. Calculate the annual habitat loss rate (% per year). Round to 2 decimal places.
templates.explanation:
Annual Habitat Loss Rate = (1 − (Final/Initial)^(1/Years)) × 100
= (1 − ([FINAL]/[INIT])^(1/[YRS])) × 100
= [RESULT]% per year

Compound habitat loss rate mirrors financial depreciation. Even a modest 2%/yr loss halves habitat in 35 years. Satellite-derived land cover datasets (e.g., Hansen Global Forest Change) now track habitat loss at 30m resolution globally in near-real time. Habitat fragmentation multiplies the impact of area loss — interior core habitat declines faster than total area.

templates.pattern: A region has a population of [POP] million and consumes [RES] tonnes of a resource per person per year. The sustainable resource supply is [SUPPLY] million tonnes per year. Calculate the resource deficit (million tonnes/yr) if any.
templates.explanation:
Resource Deficit = (Population × Per Capita Consumption) − Sustainable Supply
= ([POP] × [RES]) − [SUPPLY]
= [RESULT] million tonnes/yr

Population pressure on resources is quantified by the I=PAT framework: Environmental Impact = Population × Affluence × Technology. Even with stable population, rising affluence increases per capita consumption. Resource caps define carrying capacity — the maximum population an environment can support sustainably. Planetary boundaries define nine Earth system limits, six of which have already been transgressed.

templates.pattern: A country has an ecological footprint of [EF] global hectares (gha) per person and a biocapacity of [BC] gha per person. With a population of [POP] million, calculate the total ecological overshoot (million gha).
templates.explanation:
Ecological Overshoot = (Footprint − Biocapacity) × Population
= ([EF] − [BC]) × [POP]
= [RESULT] million gha

The ecological footprint measures how much biologically productive land/sea is required to produce resources consumed and absorb waste. Global average footprint is ~2.7 gha/person vs. biocapacity of ~1.6 gha/person — humanity currently needs 1.7 Earths. Earth Overshoot Day (the date Earth's resource budget is exhausted) now falls in late July annually.

templates.pattern: The Environmental Kuznets Curve (EKC) suggests pollution peaks then declines as income rises. A country's pollution load P = [A] + [B] × GDP − [C] × GDP². Calculate the GDP (£ thousands) at which pollution is maximised. (Use turning point: GDP_peak = B / (2 × C)). Round to 2 decimal places.
templates.explanation:
EKC Turning Point: GDP_peak = B / (2C)
= [B] / (2 × [C])
= [RESULT] £ thousands

The Environmental Kuznets Curve (EKC) hypothesis posits that as income rises, pollution first increases (industrial takeoff) then decreases (post-industrial services, environmental regulation, cleaner technology). Evidence is mixed — it holds for some local pollutants (SO₂, particulates) but not for CO₂ or biodiversity loss. Critics argue it cannot justify 'grow first, clean later' policies.

templates.pattern: A country emits [EMIS] million tonnes of CO₂ and has a GDP of [GDP] billion £. Calculate the pollution intensity (tonnes CO₂ per million £ GDP). Round to 2 decimal places.
templates.explanation:
Pollution Intensity = Emissions ÷ GDP
= [EMIS]×10⁶ tonnes ÷ [GDP]×10⁹ £
= [RESULT] tonnes CO₂ per million £

Carbon intensity of GDP is a key decoupling indicator. The UK's carbon intensity fell from ~800 tCO₂/£m GDP in 1990 to ~150 tCO₂/£m in 2022 — mainly due to the shift from coal to gas and renewables and deindustrialisation. Absolute decoupling (emissions falling while GDP grows) is required for net zero; relative decoupling (emissions growing slower than GDP) is insufficient.

templates.pattern: Converting [AREA] ha of tropical forest to agriculture releases [C_STOCK] tC/ha from soil and biomass. Calculate the CO₂ equivalent released (tonnes CO₂e). (Multiply carbon by 44/12 = 3.667 to convert to CO₂). Round to 0 decimal places.
templates.explanation:
CO₂e Released = Area × Carbon Stock × 3.667
= [AREA] × [C_STOCK] × 3.667
= [RESULT] tonnes CO₂e

Land use change (LUC) CO₂ emissions are second only to fossil fuels as a source of anthropogenic greenhouse gases. The carbon conversion factor (44/12 = 3.667) reflects the molecular mass ratio of CO₂ to C. Forest soils (particularly peat) often store more carbon than above-ground biomass — drainage of tropical peatlands for palm oil releases enormous amounts of CO₂.

templates.pattern: A cultivated field loses [LOSS] kg of soil per m² per year due to water erosion. The field area is [AREA] ha. Calculate the total annual soil loss (tonnes/yr). (1 ha = 10,000 m²)
templates.explanation:
Soil Loss = Loss Rate × Area
= [LOSS] kg/m² × [AREA] ha × 10,000 m²/ha ÷ 1,000 kg/tonne
= [RESULT] tonnes/yr

The Universal Soil Loss Equation (USLE) estimates erosion from rainfall, soil erodibility, slope, cover, and management factors. Global soil erosion rates average ~13 tonnes/ha/yr for cropland — far exceeding soil formation rates (~0.5–2 t/ha/yr). Topsoil loss reduces crop yields, increases flood risk, and degrades water quality through sedimentation. No-till farming, cover crops, and contour ploughing reduce erosion.

templates.pattern: A farm applies [FERT] kg/ha of nitrogen fertiliser to [AREA] ha of cropland. [LEACH]% of applied nitrogen leaches into waterways. Calculate the total nitrogen loading to waterways (kg N/yr).
templates.explanation:
Nitrogen Loading = Fertiliser Rate × Area × Leaching Fraction
= [FERT] × [AREA] × [LEACH]/100
= [RESULT] kg N/yr

Nitrogen leaching from agriculture is the primary cause of eutrophication in freshwater and coastal systems. Excess nitrogen drives algal blooms, oxygen depletion (hypoxia), and 'dead zones' (>500 globally). The nitrogen planetary boundary has been exceeded — humanity applies ~120 Tg N/yr in fertilisers, far above the 62 Tg/yr threshold. Precision agriculture and cover crops reduce leaching.

templates.pattern: A river receives [LOAD] tonnes of phosphorus per year from agricultural runoff. The river's natural assimilative capacity is [ASSIM] tonnes/yr. Calculate the phosphorus surplus loading (tonnes/yr) contributing to eutrophication.
templates.explanation:
Phosphorus Surplus = Total Load − Assimilative Capacity
= [LOAD] − [ASSIM]
= [RESULT] tonnes P/yr

Phosphorus is the limiting nutrient in most freshwater systems. Unlike nitrogen, phosphorus has no atmospheric reservoir — it cycles only through soils, water, and organisms. The critical threshold for eutrophication onset is ~0.02–0.05 mg/L in rivers. Phosphorus is also a finite resource — global rock phosphate reserves may be depleted within 300–400 years. Phosphorus recovery from wastewater is a key circular economy priority.

templates.pattern: A fishery has a population growth rate r = [R] yr⁻¹ and a carrying capacity K = [K] thousand tonnes. Calculate the Maximum Sustainable Yield (MSY) in thousand tonnes using MSY = r × K / 4. Round to 2 decimal places.
templates.explanation:
Maximum Sustainable Yield MSY = r × K / 4
= ([R]/100) × [K] / 4
= [RESULT] thousand tonnes

MSY is the theoretical maximum harvest that a fish stock can sustain indefinitely, occurring at half the carrying capacity (K/2) under the logistic growth model. The MSY harvest rate = r/2. In practice, MSY is difficult to achieve due to uncertainty in stock assessment, mixed fisheries, and the precautionary approach. Most fisheries managers now target biomass above BMSY to reduce collapse risk.
